Sawest
SAW-est
v. (2nd pers. sing., past t.)
The second-person singular past of see, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it as the form used with thou. Daniel and Revelation use it repeatedly as the hinge between vision and interpretation: thou sawest… and then the meaning.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sawest is the word by which an interpreter takes hold of what another man has seen and tells him what it was. Daniel uses it to recount Nebuchadnezzar’s dream before explaining it: Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image. This great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee; and the form thereof was terrible (Daniel 2:31). Daniel had not been told the dream; God gave him both the vision and its meaning, which is why the chapter proves the God of heaven against the wise men of Babylon. The decisive clause follows: Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces (Daniel 2:34) — a kingdom not raised by human hands that shatters the succession of empires. Revelation uses the form the same way as the angel interprets to John: the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings, which have received no kingdom as yet (Revelation 17:12). And Jonathan uses it to plead David’s cause before Saul, appealing to what his father had seen with his own eyes: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause? (1 Samuel 19:5). Seeing binds a man; he cannot afterward act as though he had not seen.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives SAWEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb see, used with thou: didst behold, didst perceive by the eye, didst witness.

expand to see more

SAWEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb SEE; used with the pronoun thou.

SEE, v.t. — To perceive by the eye; to behold; and in the past, to have beheld or witnessed.

To have known by observation or experience; as, thou sawest it, and didst rejoice.

In prophetic narrative, to have beheld in vision that which God presented to the mind.

From Saxon seon, to see; the past tense saw, with the second person singular ending -est.

Key Scripture

Daniel 2:31 — "Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image. This great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee; and the form thereof was terrible."

Daniel 2:34 — "Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces."

Revelation 17:12 — "And the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings, which have received no kingdom as yet; but receive power as kings one hour with the beast."

1 Samuel 19:5 — "For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?"

Modern Corruption

The late-dating of Daniel to the second century BC is not a conclusion drawn from the text but a requirement imposed by the assumption that predictive prophecy cannot happen, and it is the standard critical position taught in most universities and many seminaries.

expand to see more

The argument runs backwards from a premise. Daniel 2 and Daniel 7-11 describe the succession of empires with an accuracy that grows sharper as it approaches the Greek period, so the critical school concludes that the book must have been written after those events, around 165 BC, by an author writing history as though it were prophecy. But the accuracy is the datum, and the second-century date is the device for removing it. The dictionary holds the sixth-century date and Danielic authorship. The Lord Jesus cited Daniel the prophet by name (Matthew 24:15); the book was already in the Greek Old Testament translated in the third and second centuries; and the theory requires that a pseudonymous work produced within living memory be received as ancient Scripture by the very generation that would have known better.

What is at stake is not a date but whether God announces the future. Daniel 2:34 shows a stone cut out without hands smashing the image and becoming a mountain that fills the earth — the kingdom of God set up in the days of those kings and never destroyed. Isaiah makes prediction the very proof of deity: shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods (Isaiah 41:23). A method that rules out predictive prophecy before reading the text has decided the question of God before opening the book, and it will produce a late date for every passage that foretells anything. 1 Samuel 19:5 supplies the other application: Saul had seen David’s deliverance of Israel and rejoiced in it, and Jonathan holds him to it — envy requires a man to un-see what he has seen.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chazah (H2372), to see in vision; raah (H7200), to see, to behold; Aramaic chaza (H2370), to see, the verb of Daniel’s Aramaic chapters; Greek eido (G1492), to see, to know.

expand to see more

Aramaic chaza (H2370) — to see, to behold; the verb of Daniel 2:31 and 2:34 in the Aramaic section of the book.

Hebrew chazah (H2372) — to see in vision; the root of chozeh, a seer, and chazon, a vision.

Hebrew raah (H7200) — to see, to look upon; used of ordinary sight and of prophetic sight alike.

Greek eido (G1492) — to see and thereby to know; behind the repeated which thou sawest of Revelation 17.

Greek apokalupsis (G602) — an uncovering, a revelation; the title of the last book and the thing seeing yields.

Usage

"Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image (Daniel 2:31) — the dream recounted by a man who was never told it."

"Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands (Daniel 2:34) — the kingdom no human hand erects."

"Thou sawest it, and didst rejoice (1 Samuel 19:5) — envy requires a man to un-see what he has seen."
